chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
title: Solo pianists Fred Skinner and Harold Brown
summary: Fred Skinner played solo at the Ambassador, and Harold Brown, Lawrence Brown's brother, held long solo engagements with loyal followings.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom

blocks.x: As -- no, he was doing a single.
he was working as a single. And I must not leave out --
He plays and sings. Oh, yeah, he's a singer. A marvelous entertainer, marvelous entertainer. And as I say, he still -- he's still doing the same thing.

He still entertains. He's not living right in town, but he's a good guy too, so maybe it's time to contact him, because he's seen a lot of things, because he's always -- he has always been on top of things and worked in the very finest spots, you know, available.

Another person that was here and working as a single was Harold Brown. Now, Harold Brown, he has worked in some very fine spots in Los Angeles, as a single. He's never -- I have never known him to work with anyone, but he's always worked as a single.
Lawrence Brown's brother. And to my knowledge he probably gets on a job and stays on it longer than anybody.

That's right, and he has done this through the years, you know. It's just wonderful, but he's very competent. I mean he has a very distinct style. He's a very -- he's in command all the time, with his piano, you know.
And he has quite a following, quite a loyal following.
Whenever I've gone to see him I know the people there seem to be regulars, people who seem as though they must come every night.
